text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Anti-nuclear demonstrators throw stones and firebombs at police, errect barricades and burrow under streets leading to Gorleben. Six containers expected to be brought to Gorleben today.
- Export is key supporting point of economy, according to federal statistics office. Export in 1996 gains five percent from 1995.
- More students want to study pharmacy and medicine.
- NATO will end its mission in Bosnia in mid-1998, say U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen and German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe.
- German companies hope for foreign business demand. Ifo institute sees improvements at start of 1997.
HANDELSBLATT
- German foreign trade climbs to record levels.
- Coalition's tax plans could threaten up to 300,000 jobs in construction industry, housing construction group says in joint statement with unions and renters association.
- Daimler-Benz excites stock market with unexpectedly favourable earnings data.
- President Roman Herzog calls for Germans to be alert to dangers of racism.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG

- The massive disruptions of the nuclear waste transport to Gorleben touch off major political row between states of Lower Saxony and Bavaria. Bavaria says Lower Saxony has been too defensive about the transport and waited too long to move against demonstrators. Lower Saxony says nuclear waste should have stayed in Bavaria.
- German exports at record levels
- Bavarian wants to push through plans for motorway user fee.
DIE WELT
- Day of violence at Gorleben, protests against nuclear waste transport expand
- Tax inspectors search DG Bank headquarters in Frankfurt. Bank employees suspected of moving money to Luxembourg and evading taxes.
